source_title: Unlawful Operation of Model or Unmanned Aircraft — FAA Violation / Interference with Emergency Operations
regulated_party: Any person operating a model aircraft or civil unmanned aircraft
regulated_activity: Operating in a manner prohibited by federal aviation law/regulation, or interfering with a law enforcement, firefighter, or emergency services operation
summary: Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-3729(A) makes it unlawful to operate a model aircraft or civil unmanned aircraft if the operation (1) is prohibited by federal law or regulation governing aeronautics, including FAA regulations, or (2) interferes with a law enforcement, firefighter, or emergency services operation. A violation is a class 1 misdemeanor (up to 6 months jail, 3 years probation, and a fine up to $2,500).
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This provision effectively makes any FAA Part 107 violation a state-law violation as well — maintain rigorous Part 107 compliance (airspace authorizations, altitude limits, remote pilot certification) since a federal violation automatically triggers state criminal exposure. Do not fly near active emergency, fire, or law-enforcement operations.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document FAA compliance (certifications, authorizations, waivers) for every commercial flight, since this statute ties state criminal liability directly to federal regulatory compliance rather than creating an independent standard.
verification_status: Full current statutory text (2025 Arizona Revised Statutes) verified directly against Justia's codification.

source_title: Unlawful Operation Near Critical Facility (photographing/loitering in furtherance of a crime)
uas_topic: Critical infrastructure / correctional facility UAS restriction
regulated_party: Any person operating a UAS near a critical facility
regulated_activity: Intentionally photographing or loitering over or near a 'critical facility' in furtherance of any criminal offense; separately, flying within 500 ft horizontal or 250 ft vertical of a critical facility without written consent (per secondary-source elaboration of the buffer distance)
requirement_type: Prohibition (criminal offense); written consent from facility owner/operator is a defense
summary: Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-3729(B) makes it unlawful to operate or use a UAS to intentionally photograph or loiter over or near a 'critical facility' in furtherance of any criminal offense. 'Critical facility' (§ 13-3729(F)(3)) is defined extremely broadly to include petroleum/alumina refineries; petroleum, chemical, or rubber production/transportation/storage/processing facilities; chemical manufacturing facilities; water/wastewater treatment facilities and dams; electric generation facilities and associated substations/switchyards; electrical transmission/distribution substations; transmission lines of 69,000+ volts; communication stations/towers; energy control centers; distribution operating centers; natural gas transfer/distribution facilities including LNG facilities; railroad infrastructure; federal/state/county/municipal courts; public safety/emergency operation facilities; jails and prisons; military installations; and hospitals receiving air ambulance service. A first violation is a class 6 felony (up to 1.5 years imprisonment, fine up to $150,000); a second or subsequent violation is a class 5 felony (up to 2.5 years). Secondary sources report an accompanying 500 ft horizontal / 250 ft vertical buffer distance and a written-consent defense, elaborating on the base statutory text.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat the critical-facility list as directly relevant to nearly every AEC infrastructure project — refineries, water/wastewater plants, electrical substations and transmission lines, communications towers, railroads, courts, jails/prisons, military installations, and hospitals are all covered. Obtain the facility owner/operator's written consent before any UAS flight within (or reasonably close to) the reported 500 ft/250 ft buffer, and document that consent, since this is a felony-level offense with unusually harsh penalties compared to other states.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This is one of the harshest state-level UAS critical-infrastructure statutes reviewed to date (felony from the first offense, up to $150,000 fine) — build written-consent documentation into standard operating procedure for any Arizona project near a listed facility type, and confirm the exact 500 ft/250 ft buffer language directly against the codified statute (this record's core prohibition and facility list were independently verified; the specific buffer distances were corroborated by, but not independently re-derived from, secondary sources).
verification_status: Core prohibition, felony classification, and full 'critical facility' definition verified directly against Justia's codification of the 2025 Arizona Revised Statutes; the specific 500 ft horizontal/250 ft vertical buffer distance is corroborated by multiple secondary industry-compliance sources but was not located verbatim in the statutory subsection text obtained (which does not itself state a numeric buffer distance) — this may derive from a related provision, agency guidance, or an imprecise secondary paraphrase.
notes: High-priority item: confirm whether the 500 ft/250 ft buffer distance appears in a related statutory subsection, administrative rule, or is a secondary-source approximation of the 'over or near' standard in subsection (B), before citing a specific numeric buffer to a client.

geographic_scope: Statewide (state preemption of local UAS ordinances)
source_title: State Preemption of Local UAS Regulation
regulated_activity: Enacting or adopting any ordinance, policy, or rule relating to the ownership or operation of a UAS, or otherwise regulating UAS ownership/operation
summary: Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-3729(C) prohibits a city, town, or county from enacting or adopting any ordinance, policy, or rule relating to UAS ownership or operation, or otherwise regulating UAS ownership or operation; any such measure, whether enacted before or after August 6, 2016, is void. Subsection (D) carves out three exceptions: (1) the statute does not apply to a person/entity operating under FAA authorization consistent with that authorization or FAA rules; (2) a city/town/county may still regulate a public UAS it owns; and (3) a city/town/county may regulate takeoff/landing of a model aircraft in a park or preserve it owns, if other parks/preserves are available for model-aircraft use (or if it has only one park/preserve). Secondary sources describe this as one of the strongest state UAS-preemption clauses in the country.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Arizona's preemption is unusually strong and well-corroborated — AEC operators should generally not expect a significant municipal drone-ordinance patchwork comparable to Colorado's, though confirm whether a specific project site is a city/town/county-owned park or preserve subject to the narrow takeoff/landing carve-out.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: A local ordinance purporting to independently regulate UAS ownership or operation outside the narrow statutory exceptions is void by operation of state law; confirm this on a project-specific basis, and monitor pending legislation (see AZ-008) that would further reinforce this preemption.
verification_status: Full current statutory text (subsections C and D) verified directly against Justia's codification of the 2025 Arizona Revised Statutes.

source_title: Careless or Reckless Aircraft Operation (applicable to model/unmanned aircraft)
uas_topic: General safety restriction applicable to UAS
regulated_party: Any person operating an aircraft, including model aircraft and unmanned aircraft
regulated_activity: Careless or reckless operation of an aircraft (in the air, on the ground, or on water) in a manner that endangers the life or property of another
summary: Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 28-8280 prohibits careless or reckless operation of an aircraft — expressly including model aircraft and unmanned aircraft per secondary-source description of this section — in the air, on the ground, or on water, in a manner that endangers the life or property of another person. Courts reportedly consider federal safety standards (e.g., FAA Part 107 operating rules) when determining whether an operation was careless or reckless. A violation is a class 1 misdemeanor (up to 6 months jail, fine up to $2,500).
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Adhere strictly to Part 107 operational limits (altitude, visual line of sight, no operations over people without a waiver, etc.) since a Part 107 violation could independently support a careless/reckless state charge under this statute, layered on top of § 13-3729(A)'s FAA-violation provision.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This statute functions as a general backstop safety standard distinct from § 13-3729; document standard safety practices (pre-flight checklists, weather assessment, site risk assessment) as evidence of non-reckless operation.
verification_status: Citation, substance, and penalty confirmed via a secondary industry-compliance source; a direct fetch of this section's text from Justia's codification returned no content in this pass and the statute was not independently re-verified against the primary source.
notes: Recommend direct verification of the full current text of § 28-8280 against the Arizona Revised Statutes before citing specific language to a client.

geographic_scope: Statewide (Arizona State Parks and Trails-administered lands)
source_title: UAS Prohibition in State Parks (Recreational); Filming Permit Required for Commercial Use
citation: ASPT Agency Policy (Frequently Asked Questions, 'Can I use my drone/plane (Quadcopter/UAV) in a state park?')
revision_date: Current — subject to ASPT review as laws/technology change
regulated_activity: Launching, landing, or operating a UAS on Arizona State Parks and Trails property
summary: Arizona State Parks and Trails' published policy states that all recreational drone use is currently prohibited in state parks. Commercial UAS use will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis through a Filming Permit for news, publicity, and promotional purposes; Filming Permit rules require liability insurance and a current FAA drone registration, with the final decision and any associated fees at the discretion of park management. Access to areas beyond a park's boundary (National Forest, State Trust Land, Game and Fish Department land, and other agencies) may require additional permits from those agencies. ASPT states it will evaluate updates to this policy as laws, rules, and technology change.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Apply for an ASPT Filming Permit well in advance of any commercial AEC UAS work (inspection, mapping, documentation) planned within a state park boundary, and budget for park-management discretion over the final decision and fees; confirm separately with any adjoining land-management agency (National Forest, State Trust Land, Game and Fish) if the project area extends beyond the park boundary.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the Filming Permit, proof of liability insurance, and FAA registration documentation in the project file for any state-park UAS work; monitor ASPT's policy for updates given the agency's own statement that the rule is subject to change.
verification_status: Policy text read directly and in full from Arizona State Parks and Trails' own published FAQ page.

source_title: Prohibition on Using Drones to Harass, Pursue, or Aid in Taking Wildlife
citation: Ariz. Admin. Code R12-4-320; Ariz. Rev. Stat. §§ 17-301, 17-239
regulated_activity: Using a drone (or other aircraft, or motorized terrestrial/aquatic vehicle) to harass, molest, chase, rally, concentrate, herd, intercept, torment, or drive wildlife
requirement_type: Prohibition, with exceptions for A.R.S. § 17-239-compliant activity and authorized state/federal employees acting within official duties
summary: Ariz. Admin. Code R12-4-320(A) makes it unlawful, in addition to the provisions of A.R.S. § 17-301, to harass, molest, chase, rally, concentrate, herd, intercept, torment, or drive wildlife with or from any aircraft — expressly including drones, as defined under R12-4-301 — or with or from any motorized terrestrial or aquatic vehicle. Subsection (B) exempts persons acting in accordance with A.R.S. § 17-239, and persons acting within the scope of official duties as a state or federal employee/authorized agent managing or protecting land, water, wildlife, livestock, domesticated animals, human life, or crops. Secondary sources further describe a 48-hour pre-season scouting restriction for big game (mirroring rules for airplanes/helicopters) and a narrow exception permitting drone use to help recover already-lawfully-harvested big game, provided no one in the party is actively hunting during the recovery flight.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Plan environmental-monitoring, habitat-mapping, or resource-inventory UAS flights to avoid any activity that could be read as harassing, chasing, herding, or otherwise disturbing wildlife, and build a conservative standoff buffer near known wildlife concentrations, particularly during the 48-hour pre-season window before big-game hunting seasons.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the survey/mapping purpose of any UAS flight over wildlife habitat to distinguish it from a prohibited harassment or hunting-assistance use; the official-duty exception in R12-4-320(B)(2) may be relevant context for AEC firms performing wildlife-management-related work under contract with a state or federal agency.
verification_status: Full current regulatory text verified directly against Justia's codification of the Arizona Administrative Code (current through the June 20, 2025 register); the 48-hour pre-season scouting restriction and harvested-game recovery exception are corroborated by secondary sources but were not located verbatim in R12-4-320 itself and may derive from a related Game and Fish Commission order or hunting regulation.

summary: The Arizona State Board of Technical Registration licenses and regulates engineers, land surveyors, geologists, landscape architects, and other technical professions under Title 32, Chapter 1, C.R.S. Arizona statutes and BTR rules generally require licensees to practice only within their demonstrated competency. No standalone BTR rule, advisory, or guidance document specifically addressing UAS-derived photogrammetry, LiDAR, or mapping products was located during this research pass.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Route UAS-derived photogrammetry/LiDAR mapping products through an Arizona-licensed PE or PLS for review under the existing general competency framework before delivery on any official survey or engineering deliverable, since no Arizona-specific UAS board standard currently exists to follow instead.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document licensed-professional review and QA/QC of UAS-derived deliverables given the absence of Arizona-specific UAS guidance; consider a direct inquiry to BTR for novel UAS-derived-product certification questions.
verification_status: General agency framework confirmed via BTR's own website; the specific UAS-related competency-rule language commonly cited for other states (the 'Rule 415' pattern) was not located as an Arizona-specific citation and is not asserted here.
notes: Recommend direct verification of current BTR rules (Arizona Administrative Code Title 4, Chapter 30) before citing a specific rule number to a client.
